extracted.intended_audience: Associate Editors (and prospective AEs) of The American Naturalist; journal editors
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and normative guidance for Associate Editors at The American Naturalist on triaging manuscripts, soliciting and interpreting reviews, writing decision letters, and managing revisions to provide a high-quality, constructive peer-review experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know the journal's editorial style and tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Associate Editors are expected to know the journal's editorial style from having been reviewers and authors, and to follow practical procedures (e.g., how to use Editorial Manager).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AE orientation includes familiarity with the journal's editorial norms and the practical mechanics of the submission system (Editorial Manager). These procedural competencies are assumed but also provided in detailed guidelines when joining the editorial board.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial triage: read carefully and decide whether to use reviewer time
rubrics_metrics.description: Look at the paper carefully before review, and decide if it is worth using reviewer time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take notes on first read to help later with writing a decision letter. The AE should form an early judgment about importance and fatal flaws so reviewers' time is allocated efficiently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write clear editorial declines when not sending to reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: If you believe it is not a sufficiently important advance, or has flaws that will raise serious barriers to publication, write a review that clearly explains your logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial declines without review (by AE or Editor) should include enough of a review so authors are convinced the paper was read carefully, and should contain enough feedback that authors feel the submission was worthwhile because it helps them adjust approach for the next journal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use DWOP (Decline Without Prejudice) for high-potential but fixable manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: When a paper has real but unrealized potential, send it back with a clear statement of what the value of the paper could be and what needs to happen to realize that potential (DWOP).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply DWOP selectively to papers with high value that would likely meet avoidable reviewer resistance; provide concrete pre-review feedback so authors can improve before sending to reviewers, and thereby save reviewers' time and increase chances of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: AE should write an independent synthesis when reviews arrive
rubrics_metrics.description: When reviews come in, write a review of your own after reading reviewers and revisiting the manuscript and your notes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AE's review should include: (a) the AE's own feedback on points reviewers may have missed; (b) a summary of essential points from reviewers (and the AE's own reading) that preclude further consideration or must be dealt with in revision; (c) arbitration between conflicting reviews, done respectfully and acting as a buffer between authors and overly aggressive or negative reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arbitrate reviewer disagreements respectfully and protect authors from harsh reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: If you disagree with reviewers or need to arbitrate between conflicting reviews, do so while being respectful to the reviewers and buffering the authors from mean or thoughtless reviewer language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide considered judgments when reviewers ask for unreasonable items or express themselves poorly; the AE acts as an arbiter and should moderate tone and expectations in communication to authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Look for 'diamonds in the rough' and invest editorial effort when warranted
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep a lookout for papers with a great underlying idea or unique dataset that might get negative reviews in current form but could become excellent with work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delve deeply into such manuscripts rather than knee-jerk declining; thoughtful AE engagement and careful recommendation letters can guide authors through revisions that transform a rough submission into a high-impact paper (example cited: Meg Duffy story).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid endless revision cycles; decline when unlikely to improve sufficiently
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess likelihood that authors can address major concerns after the first round of review or first revision, and recommend 'decline' for papers unlikely to improve sufficiently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not prolong multiple rounds of revision and re-review unnecessarily. Authors are often most upset when papers are declined after two or more rounds; weigh prospects for meaningful improvement early and be willing to stop the cycle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept Editors' oversight and the need to manage acceptance rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that the three Editors actively assess papers and reviews and may disagree with AE recommendations or change recommendations to manage overall acceptance rates and print flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not be offended if Editors nudge recommendations (e.g., Major Revision ↔ DWAP, DWOP ↔ Decline); Editors may discuss manuscripts to reach consensus or make adjustments for journal-level editorial management (backlog, issue composition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance pushing for clearer writing with preserving authors' voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Find the right balance between pushing authors to improve their writing while allowing them to retain their own voice as writers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guide authors through improving difficult prose when necessary, because clarity can determine readership and impact, but avoid forcing authors to adopt your personal stylistic preferences when their original, readable style is sound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make timely, independent decisions without unnecessary re-review
rubrics_metrics.description: You don't always need to take reviewers' time, especially on a revision; read the response letter and manuscript and make a decision if the authors satisfied reviewers' concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If authors have made substantial technical changes that the AE cannot evaluate, send the revision back out for review; otherwise the AE should attempt to reach a final decision after checking for any remaining concerns. See linked prior post for more on re-review and DWOP/Decline distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide substantive, non-cursory decision letters that add AE insight
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid writing relatively cursory decision letters that mostly summarize reviewers' points; strive to add at least a few insights of your own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When AEs and Editors add their own considered opinions (rather than simply echoing reviewers), authors feel they received a fair evaluation and are more likely to improve their work. Allocate time to contribute unique, constructive guidance in decision letters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim to add value to authors' work by improving clarity, accuracy, interpretation, or data
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviews and decision letters should push authors to improve the clarity of their writing, the accuracy of their analysis and interpretation, or to add key data—thereby contributing to the quality of the published literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A productive editorial contribution may result in stronger papers even if the manuscript is ultimately published elsewhere; constructive, clear feedback that helps authors rethink approaches is a mark of success for the journal's review process.
